analysis.one_liner: Stops companies from forcing consumers and workers into private arbitration for legal rights claims.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill with 15 Democratic cosponsors to let people take statutory claims to court instead of forced arbitration died in the Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any floor action before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies routinely write clauses into employment, credit card, cell phone, and nursing home contracts requiring customers and employees to settle legal disputes in private arbitration, often one case at a time, rather than in court. This bill would change federal arbitration law so that no pre-dispute arbitration clause can block an individual or small business from going to court over a violation of a federal or state law or a constitution, and it would let state rules against unfair contract terms apply. A court, not the arbitrator, would decide whether an arbitration agreement is enforceable. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, employees, and small businesses who sign contracts containing arbitration clauses. The bill would give them a path back to open court when a company violates a law that protects them, instead of having that choice made for them in the fine print before any dispute exists. It would also restore the ability of state legislatures to shield their residents from unfair arbitration terms.

how_it_helps.text: Invalidates pre-dispute arbitration clauses that block an individual or small business from bringing a claim for damages or an injunction arising from an alleged violation of a federal or state statute, the U.S. Constitution, or a state constitution; only an agreement made after the dispute arises would be honored.

States that courts may refuse to enforce an arbitration agreement on any ground of contract law or public policy, including unconscionability or a lack of a true meeting of the minds, under federal or state statutes or court findings.
Puts the decision about whether an arbitration agreement is enforceable in the hands of a judge rather than the arbitrator the company selected.
Allows an arbitration award to be thrown out if the arbitration took place in violation of the new rule, adding enforcement teeth.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that embed arbitration clauses in standard-form contracts — banks and credit card issuers, telecom firms, employers, nursing homes, and similar consumer-facing businesses — would face lawsuits in open court and renewed exposure to class actions, and could pass some of those legal costs on to customers through prices and fees.

drawbacks.text: The bill is narrower than it may sound: it only protects claims based on a violation of a statute or constitution. Ordinary contract disputes not grounded in a legal right could still be forced into arbitration under the same clauses.

Businesses argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper than litigation for small individual disputes, and that court cases and class actions can take years and deliver most of their value to lawyers rather than to the people harmed.
Reopening courthouse doors for statutory claims would raise litigation costs for a broad range of companies, some of which would be passed along to consumers in prices and fees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: as things stand, someone with a legally protected claim can be required to pursue it alone, in a private forum chosen by the company they are suing. The bill's honest limits are that it leaves ordinary contract disputes in arbitration and that litigation is slow and expensive, so getting to court is not the same as winning. Weighing those, the bill addresses a genuine imbalance at a modest, defensible cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and that is where it sat — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — until the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 7, 2017 by Sen. Patrick Leahy with 14 other Democratic senators as original cosponsors.
On the day of introduction it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 115th Congress.
Fifteen senators are listed as cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on forced arbitration clauses in standard-form contracts — banks, telecoms, employers, nursing homes, and arbitration providers — kept a system in which disputes are resolved privately and one at a time, because the bill never advanced far enough for a vote.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and submitted findings that recent Supreme Court arbitration decisions have left millions of people unable to vindicate rights in court.

for.name: 15 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled it for consideration; it received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats and none acted on the bill in committee or on the floor; no Republican supported it, and the Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee took no action on it after the referral.

industries.industry: Consumer-facing corporations (banks, credit card issuers, telecoms, employers, nursing homes)
industries.note: These companies embed pre-dispute arbitration clauses in standard-form contracts, which the bill would make unenforceable for statutory claims. Their interest in keeping those clauses runs directly against the public's ability to sue over violations of the law.

Arbitration firms are paid largely by companies that mandate arbitration; invalidating those mandates for consumer and employment claims shrinks the market that keeps them in that role. Their business interest depends on the arrangement the bill would limit.
Restoring court access for statutory claims reopens demand for courtroom representation of consumers and workers. Their gain coincides with the public's restored access to court.
